label: M9 S13 | The Complete Analytical Workflow — Formula Hierarchy by Laye

formulas.name: LAYER 2: Profitability & Returns Arsenal
formulas.formula: Critical metrics: (1) Revenue Growth = (Current Revenue - Prior Revenue)/Prior Revenue × 100; (2) Operating Margin = EBIT/Revenue × 100; (3) Net Margin = Net Profit/Revenue × 100; (4) ROE = Net Profit/Equity × 100 (DuPont decomposed); (5) ROCE = EBIT/Capital Employed × 100

variables.meaning: Earnings Before Interest and Tax — operating profit
Equity + Long-term Debt — the capital base funding business operations
(Opening Equity + Closing Equity)/2 — used for ROE

formulas.worked_example: TCS FY23: Revenue Growth = 13.7%; Operating Margin = 24.1%; Net Margin = 19.2%; ROE = 45.3%; ROCE = 46.1%. HUL FY23: Revenue Growth = 15.0%; Operating Margin = 24.0%; Net Margin = 17.1%; ROE = 22.1%; ROCE = 25.8%. Both companies have similar Operating Margins, but vastly different ROE. Why? TCS has higher leverage (implied by the DuPont ratio difference) and asset efficiency. Applying the DuPont framework: ROE = Net Margin × Asset Turnover × Equity Multiplier. TCS: 19.2% × 2.8 × 1.5 ≈ 45.3%. HUL: 17.1% × 2.2 × 1.2 ≈ 22.1%. Same margin, different ratios show different business dynamics.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Always compute these alongside 5-year trends. A company with stable margin but declining Revenue Growth is in a growth deceleration phase that will eventually compress margins. A company with expanding margin but flat Revenue is near-term efficient but long-term growth-challenged.

formulas.name: LAYER 3: Balance Sheet Health Ratios
formulas.formula: Critical metrics: (1) Current Ratio = Current Assets/Current Liabilities; (2) Debt/Equity = Total Debt/Total Equity; (3) Interest Coverage Ratio = EBIT/Interest Expense; (4) Net Debt/EBITDA = (Total Debt - Cash)/EBITDA; (5) CCC = DIO + DSO - DPO

variables.meaning: Short-term assets: cash + receivables + inventory + prepaid + other
Short-term debt + long-term debt + current portion of LT debt
DIO = (Inventory × 365)/COGS; DSO = (Receivables × 365)/Revenue; DPO = (Payables × 365)/COGS

formulas.worked_example: HUL FY23 Balance Sheet Health: Current Ratio = 1.5; Quick Ratio = 1.2; Debt/Equity = 0.05 (essentially zero); Interest Coverage = 50+ (interest expense minimal); Net Debt/EBITDA = near zero; DIO = 35 days; DSO = 18 days; DPO = 60 days; CCC = 35 + 18 - 60 = -7 days (NEGATIVE — strong working capital moat). Compare an Indian capital goods company: Current Ratio = 1.8; Quick Ratio = 1.1; Debt/Equity = 0.45; Interest Coverage = 6; Net Debt/EBITDA = 2.5; DIO = 90 days; DSO = 85 days; DPO = 60 days; CCC = 90 + 85 - 60 = 115 days (115 days of capital locked in working capital).
formulas.sensitivity_note: The 120-day CCC difference between HUL and the capital goods company explains enormous differences in cash flow quality, valuation premium, and investor preference. Working capital dynamics can be more decisive than margin differences for long-term value creation.

formulas.name: LAYER 4: Cash Flow Quality Ratios
formulas.formula: Critical metrics: (1) OCF / Net Profit Ratio (3-5 year average); (2) Free Cash Flow = OCF - Capex; (3) Cash Conversion Ratio = FCF/Net Profit × 100; (4) FCF Yield = FCF/Market Cap × 100; (5) FCF Margin = FCF/Revenue × 100

variables.meaning: Cash generated from operations, before capex
Capital expenditure for maintaining and growing assets
Total market value of equity

formulas.worked_example: Asian Paints FY23: OCF = ₹5,200 Cr; Net Profit = ₹4,106 Cr; OCF/Net Profit = 127%. FCF = 5,200 - 600 (capex) = ₹4,600 Cr. Cash Conversion = 4,600/4,106 = 112%. FCF Yield ≈ 1.7% at market cap ₹2,75,000 Cr. FCF Margin = 4,600/25,000 = 18.4%. Elite metrics — FCF exceeds Net Profit (negative working capital), strong cash yield. Contrast with a capex-heavy auto component maker: OCF/Net Profit might be 78%; FCF negative due to heavy capex; Cash Conversion 45%. Dramatic difference in cash quality.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Always compute 5-year rolling averages of these metrics. A company with current-year OCF/Net Profit of 110% but 5-year average of 65% has significant reversal — the current year may be unsustainable. Consistency matters more than any single year.

formulas.name: LAYER 5: Valuation & Positioning Metrics
formulas.formula: Critical metrics: (1) P/E = Price per Share/EPS (or Market Cap/Net Profit); (2) EV/EBITDA = Enterprise Value/EBITDA; (3) Price/Book = Market Cap/Shareholders Equity; (4) PEG Ratio = P/E/Earnings Growth Rate; (5) Dividend Yield = Dividend/Price × 100

variables.meaning: Earnings Per Share = Net Profit/Shares Outstanding
Market Cap + Debt - Cash — total enterprise value
Expected EPS growth rate, typically 3-5 year forward

formulas.worked_example: HUL FY23: P/E (TTM) = 55; EV/EBITDA = 36; Price/Book = 60; PEG Ratio = 55/12 = 4.6 (expensive on PEG); Dividend Yield = 1.5%. TCS FY23: P/E = 28; EV/EBITDA = 22; Price/Book = 15; PEG = 28/9 = 3.1; Dividend Yield = 1.2%. Applying comparative analysis: HUL trades at premium to TCS despite lower growth, because HUL is structurally more profitable and has better moat. Industry benchmarks: FMCG median P/E ~40x; HUL premium reflects top-quartile operational positioning. IT services median P/E ~25x; TCS premium for execution excellence. Both valuations reflect their operational positioning.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Valuation should never be analyzed in isolation. Always connect to Layer 2-4 performance: if a premium multiple requires sustained high ROE/ROCE (Layer 2) and strong cash conversion (Layer 4), the multiple is defensible. If a premium multiple assumes growth that isn't visible in Layer 3 (balance sheet can't support growth) or isn't cash-backed in Layer 4 (OCF weak), the multiple is risky.

formulas.name: The Integrated Synthesis Formula
formulas.formula: Investment Thesis = Layer 2 (profitability story) + Layer 3 (balance sheet resilience) + Layer 4 (cash quality validation) + Layer 5 (valuation justification) + Sector-Specific Context + Risks to Monitor

variables.meaning: Primary operational conclusion: what makes this business generate returns?
Financial resilience: is the business durable under stress?
Earnings reality: is the reported profit backed by cash?
Market pricing: is current valuation justified by the fundamentals?
Coherent investment thesis with action recommendation

formulas.worked_example: HUL Integrated Thesis: Layer 2 shows elite operational metrics (24% margin, 22% ROE, 25% ROCE) driven by brand moat and scale. Layer 3 shows fortress balance sheet (D/E 0.05, negative working capital). Layer 4 shows superior cash quality (OCF/NP 104%, FCF Yield 2%). Layer 5 shows premium valuation (55x P/E, PEG 4.6). Synthesis: Defensive compounder with premium pricing. Recommendation: Maintain overweight for quality-focused mandates; moderate position size due to full valuation; target return 10-12% annually via earnings growth, not multiple expansion. Risks: rural demand deceleration, input cost inflation, competitive pressure. This is a coherent investment thesis emerging from the integrated framework.
formulas.sensitivity_note: The synthesis should be specific and actionable. Generic conclusions like 'HUL is a good company' don't help. Specific conclusions like 'HUL warrants 55x P/E because operational metrics are in top-quartile across all layers, and the premium reflects durable moat' are actionable. Always aim for specific over generic.

formulas.name: LAYER 2: Profitability & Returns Arsenal
formulas.formula: Critical metrics: (1) Revenue Growth = (Current Revenue - Prior Revenue)/Prior Revenue × 100; (2) Operating Margin = EBIT/Revenue × 100; (3) Net Margin = Net Profit/Revenue × 100; (4) ROE = Net Profit/Equity × 100 (DuPont decomposed); (5) ROCE = EBIT/Capital Employed × 100

variables.meaning: Earnings Before Interest and Tax — operating profit
Total sales income for the period
Profit after all expenses, tax, and interest
Shareholders' equity or net worth
Equity + Long-term Debt — the capital base funding business operations
(Opening Equity + Closing Equity)/2 — used for ROE

formulas.plain_english: These metrics reveal how efficiently a business converts sales into profit and how effectively it deploys shareholder capital. Revenue Growth shows top-line momentum; Operating and Net Margins show how much profit remains at each income statement layer. ROE and ROCE answer the core question: how much return is the business generating on the capital invested in it? An expanding margin paired with slowing growth signals operational excellence but potential long-term stagnation.

worked_example.problem: Compare profitability and capital efficiency of two FMCG leaders in FY23.
steps: TCS FY23 reported: Revenue Growth 13.7%, Operating Margin 24.1%, Net Margin 19.2%, ROE 45.3%, ROCE 46.1%
HUL FY23 reported: Revenue Growth 15.0%, Operating Margin 24.0%, Net Margin 17.1%, ROE 22.1%, ROCE 25.8%
Apply DuPont decomposition to ROE: ROE = Net Margin × Asset Turnover × Equity Multiplier
Interpret: Both have similar Operating Margins but vastly different ROE. TCS achieves higher returns through superior asset turnover and strategic leverage.
worked_example.result: TCS ROE (45.3%) is 2× HUL ROE (22.1%) despite similar operating margin, because TCS has higher asset efficiency and optimal capital structure.
worked_example.insight: Two companies with identical operating margins can generate vastly different shareholder returns. TCS's superior ROE reflects better working capital management, asset utilization, and judicious use of debt—not superior core business profitability. This distinction is critical for positioning capital-intensive versus asset-light business models.

formulas.sensitivity_note: Always compute these alongside 5-year trends. A company with stable margin but declining Revenue Growth is in a growth deceleration phase that will eventually compress margins. A company with expanding margin but flat Revenue is near-term efficient but long-term growth-challenged.

formulas.name: LAYER 3: Balance Sheet Health Ratios
formulas.formula: Critical metrics: (1) Current Ratio = Current Assets/Current Liabilities; (2) Debt/Equity = Total Debt/Total Equity; (3) Interest Coverage Ratio = EBIT/Interest Expense; (4) Net Debt/EBITDA = (Total Debt - Cash)/EBITDA; (5) CCC = DIO + DSO - DPO

variables.meaning: Short-term assets: cash + receivables + inventory + prepaid + other
Short-term obligations due within 12 months
Short-term debt + long-term debt + current portion of LT debt
Shareholders' equity or net worth
Cost of debt servicing
Earnings Before Interest, Tax, Depreciation, and Amortization
Cash and cash equivalents
DIO = (Inventory × 365)/COGS; DSO = (Receivables × 365)/Revenue; DPO = (Payables × 365)/COGS
Days Inventory Outstanding — how long inventory sits before sale
Days Sales Outstanding — average collection period
Days Payable Outstanding — average payment period to suppliers

formulas.plain_english: These ratios measure financial resilience and working capital efficiency. Liquidity ratios (Current Ratio, Debt/Equity, Interest Coverage) tell you whether a company can weather downturns and service obligations. The Cash Conversion Cycle reveals whether working capital is a source of cash (negative CCC = moat) or a capital drain (positive CCC = burden). A company with negative CCC collects before it pays—a structural advantage in any downturn.

worked_example.problem: Assess balance sheet strength and working capital moat between HUL and a typical capital goods company.
steps: HUL FY23: Current Ratio 1.5, Quick Ratio 1.2, Debt/Equity 0.05, Interest Coverage 50+, Net Debt/EBITDA near zero
Calculate HUL CCC: DIO 35 days, DSO 18 days, DPO 60 days → CCC = 35 + 18 - 60 = -7 days
Benchmark: Capital goods company with Current Ratio 1.8, Quick Ratio 1.1, Debt/Equity 0.45, Interest Coverage 6, Net Debt/EBITDA 2.5
Calculate CCC: DIO 90 days, DSO 85 days, DPO 60 days → CCC = 90 + 85 - 60 = 115 days
Compare the 122-day CCC differential: HUL generates cash from operations; capital goods company locks ₹115 of working capital per ₹365 of revenue
worked_example.result: HUL has fortress balance sheet (minimal debt, strong liquidity, negative CCC) versus capital goods company with moderate leverage but 115-day cash cycle burden.
worked_example.insight: The 115-day working capital difference explains HUL's superior valuation multiple, investor preference, and ability to weather inflation cycles. FMCG brands collect quickly (retail/e-commerce) and pay suppliers on extended terms (volume leverage), creating a structural cash-generation moat unavailable to capital goods companies.

formulas.sensitivity_note: The 120-day CCC difference between HUL and the capital goods company explains enormous differences in cash flow quality, valuation premium, and investor preference. Working capital dynamics can be more decisive than margin differences for long-term value creation.

formulas.name: LAYER 4: Cash Flow Quality Ratios
formulas.formula: Critical metrics: (1) OCF / Net Profit Ratio (3-5 year average); (2) Free Cash Flow = OCF - Capex; (3) Cash Conversion Ratio = FCF/Net Profit × 100; (4) FCF Yield = FCF/Market Cap × 100; (5) FCF Margin = FCF/Revenue × 100

variables.meaning: Cash generated from operations, before capex
Profit reported in income statement
Capital expenditure for maintaining and growing assets
OCF - Capex — cash available for debt repayment, dividends, buybacks
Total market value of equity
Total sales income

formulas.plain_english: Cash flow quality ratios distinguish genuine earnings from accounting profits. A company reporting high Net Profit but low OCF is generating earnings on paper, not in cash—a red flag. FCF (Operating Cash minus maintenance capex) is the cash truly available to shareholders. An OCF/Net Profit ratio above 100% signals efficient working capital management; below 70% warrants investigation. FCF Yield and Margin show cash-generation intensity relative to size and sales.

worked_example.problem: Evaluate cash generation quality of Asian Paints versus a capex-heavy auto component supplier.
steps: Asian Paints FY23: OCF ₹5,200 Cr, Net Profit ₹4,106 Cr, Capex ₹600 Cr, Market Cap ₹2,75,000 Cr, Revenue ₹25,000 Cr
Calculate OCF/NP: 5,200 / 4,106 = 127% (negative working capital benefit)
Calculate FCF: 5,200 - 600 = ₹4,600 Cr; Cash Conversion: 4,600 / 4,106 = 112%
Contrast auto components: OCF/NP 78%, FCF negative due to heavy capex needs, Cash Conversion 45%
worked_example.result: Asian Paints converts 112% of reported profit to free cash flow (cash exceeds earnings). Auto component supplier converts only 45%, with negative FCF after capex—no cash available for shareholders.
worked_example.insight: Asian Paints' superior metrics reflect a capital-light business model (distribution-based, no manufacturing capex) with strong working capital dynamics. Auto suppliers face structural capex burdens (tooling, machinery) that consume cash despite profitability. For equity investors, Asian Paints' cash metrics are far more attractive for sustainable dividends and shareholder returns.

formulas.sensitivity_note: Always compute 5-year rolling averages of these metrics. A company with current-year OCF/Net Profit of 110% but 5-year average of 65% has significant reversal — the current year may be unsustainable. Consistency matters more than any single year.

formulas.name: LAYER 5: Valuation & Positioning Metrics
formulas.formula: Critical metrics: (1) P/E = Price per Share/EPS (or Market Cap/Net Profit); (2) EV/EBITDA = Enterprise Value/EBITDA; (3) Price/Book = Market Cap/Shareholders Equity; (4) PEG Ratio = P/E/Earnings Growth Rate; (5) Dividend Yield = Dividend/Price × 100

variables.meaning: Current market price of one share
Earnings Per Share = Net Profit/Shares Outstanding
Share Price × Shares Outstanding
Market Cap + Total Debt - Cash
Earnings Before Interest, Tax, Depreciation, and Amortization
Book value of equity
Expected EPS growth rate, typically 3-5 year forward CAGR
Annual cash dividend paid to shareholder

formulas.plain_english: Valuation multiples answer whether the market price reflects fair value given the business quality. P/E and EV/EBITDA compare price to earnings; Price/Book compares price to accounting net worth. PEG Ratio adjusts P/E for growth, helping distinguish expensive-but-justified from expensive-and-risky. Dividend Yield shows cash income to shareholders. None of these multiples is meaningful in isolation—always tie valuation to Layer 2 (quality), Layer 3 (durability), and Layer 4 (cash backing).

worked_example.problem: Compare and justify valuation multiples of HUL versus TCS against their operational positioning.
steps: HUL FY23: P/E (TTM) 55, EV/EBITDA 36, Price/Book 60, Forward EPS Growth 12%, PEG = 55/12 = 4.6, Dividend Yield 1.5%
TCS FY23: P/E 28, EV/EBITDA 22, Price/Book 15, Forward EPS Growth 9%, PEG = 28/9 = 3.1, Dividend Yield 1.2%
Benchmark against peers: FMCG sector median P/E ~40x, IT services median P/E ~25x
Synthesize with Layer 2-4 findings: HUL (24% margin, 25% ROCE, fortress balance sheet) commands 37% premium to sector P/E; TCS (19.2% margin, 46% ROCE, strong cash) commands 12% premium
Conclusion: HUL premium justified by superior moat (brand, distribution, working capital); TCS premium modest because IT services sector is commoditizing
worked_example.result: HUL P/E of 55x is expensive on absolute basis but justified by top-quartile operational metrics and durability. TCS P/E of 28x is moderate but requires sustained growth to justify; if growth decelerates, multiple compression likely.
worked_example.insight: Valuation multiples alone are meaningless. HUL's 55x P/E looks excessive until you link it to 25% ROCE, -7-day CCC, and 24% margins—all in top decile. This is expensive-but-justified. TCS's 28x requires 9%+ EPS growth to remain fair; miss growth targets and the multiple re-rates downward sharply. Always connect multiples to fundamentals.

formulas.sensitivity_note: Valuation should never be analyzed in isolation. Always connect to Layer 2-4 performance: if a premium multiple requires sustained high ROE/ROCE (Layer 2) and strong cash conversion (Layer 4), the multiple is defensible. If a premium multiple assumes growth that isn't visible in Layer 3 (balance sheet can't support growth) or isn't cash-backed in Layer 4 (OCF weak), the multiple is risky.

formulas.name: The Integrated Synthesis Formula
formulas.formula: Investment Thesis = Layer 2 (profitability story) + Layer 3 (balance sheet resilience) + Layer 4 (cash quality validation) + Layer 5 (valuation justification) + Sector-Specific Context + Risks to Monitor

variables.meaning: Primary operational conclusion: what makes this business generate returns?
Financial resilience: is the business durable under stress?
Earnings reality: is the reported profit backed by cash?
Market pricing: is current valuation justified by the fundamentals?
Industry-specific dynamics: growth rate, competitive intensity, regulatory environment, cyclicality
Key variables that could invalidate the thesis if they deteriorate
Coherent investment thesis with action recommendation

formulas.plain_english: This is the pinnacle formula: it forces integration of all four analytical layers into a single, defensible investment thesis. No layer should be ignored; all four must tell a consistent story. If Layer 2 shows great profitability but Layer 4 shows weak cash backing, the thesis is fragile. If Layer 3 shows financial stress that contradicts Layer 2 returns, something is wrong. The Synthesis forces you to reconcile all evidence and reach a specific, actionable recommendation—not a generic conclusion.

worked_example.problem: Construct an integrated investment thesis for HUL from all four analytical layers.
steps: Layer 2 Analysis: Operating Margin 24%, Net Margin 17.1%, ROCE 25.8%, ROE 22.1%—top-quartile profitability driven by brand moat and scale economies
Layer 3 Analysis: Debt/Equity 0.05, Current Ratio 1.5, CCC -7 days—fortress balance sheet with structural working capital moat; zero financial distress risk
Layer 4 Analysis: OCF/Net Profit 104%, FCF Yield 2%, FCF Margin 18%—superior cash generation; reported profit is real cash
Layer 5 Analysis: P/E 55, EV/EBITDA 36, PEG 4.6, Dividend Yield 1.5%—premium valuation justified by Layer 2-4 quality metrics
Sector Context: FMCG sector growing 8-10% CAGR; HUL growing 15% (outpacing sector); rural demand accelerating; input cost inflation stable
Risk Factors: Rural demand deceleration (macro risk), input cost inflation (near-term pressure), competitive intensity (e-commerce pressure), foreign exchange (raw material imports)

Synthesis: HUL is a defensive compounder with durable competitive advantages (brand, distribution, working capital) reflected in premium but justified valuation. Thesis favors quality-focused long-term mandates; position sizing should reflect full valuation and limited multiple expansion upside.
worked_example.result: HUL Integrated Investment Thesis: DEFENSIVE COMPOUNDER. Maintain overweight; target 10-12% annual returns via earnings growth (not multiple expansion); position size 3-5% of portfolio. Key monitoring points: quarterly rural volume trends (growth inflection risk), input cost inflation (margin pressure), e-commerce channel mix (distribution risk).
worked_example.insight: The integrated thesis is coherent: all four layers support each other. Layer 2 (elite returns) is enabled by Layer 3 (balance sheet moat). Layer 4 (strong cash) validates Layer 2 profitability. Layer 5 (premium valuation) is justified by Layers 2-3-4. This coherence is what separates conviction theses from speculative ones. A coherent thesis allows you to hold through volatility; incoherent theses crack under pressure.

formulas.sensitivity_note: The synthesis should be specific and actionable. Generic conclusions like 'HUL is a good company' don't help. Specific conclusions like 'HUL warrants 55x P/E because operational metrics are in top-quartile across all layers, and the premium reflects durable moat' are actionable. Always aim for specific over generic.
